steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   → Extra –OH in RNA makes it more reactive and less chemically stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
   • RNA: A, G, C, Uracil (U) replaces thymine.  
   → Uracil is energetically cheaper to make; thymine helps DNA repair systems recognize damaged cytosine.

3. Strandedness & structure  
   • DNA: Typically double-stranded helix (antiparallel strands held by A-T and G-C base pairing).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded, but can fold back on itself to form hairpins, loops, and complex 3-D shapes (e.g., tRNA, rRNA).  

4. Size & length  
   • DNA molecules are long (millions of base pairs), forming chromosomes.  
   • RNA molecules are comparatively short—anywhere from ~20 nucleotides (miRNA) to several thousand (mRNA, rRNA).

5. Stability  
   • DNA: Chemically stable, can persist for decades or longer; suited for long-term genetic storage.  
   • RNA: Prone to hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation; ideal for transient messages and regulatory roles.

6. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to the nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes); small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions throughout cell—mRNA travels to cytoplasm, rRNA in ribosomes, tRNA shuttles amino acids, etc.

7. Biological roles  
   DNA:  
     – Permanent repository of hereditary information.  
     – Template for replication and transcription.  
   RNA:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): conveys genetic code to ribosomes.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): catalytic core of ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids during translation.  
     – Regulatory/structural RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, snRNA, lncRNA, etc.): gene silencing, splicing, and other controls.  
     – Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2).

8. Replication & turnover  
   • DNA is duplicated by DNA polymerases with proofreading, ensuring fidelity.  
   • RNA is synthesized by RNA polymerases; errors tolerated at higher frequency because RNA is short-lived and not heritable.

Summary  
DNA is the durable, double-stranded, thymine-containing molecule optimized for long-term storage of genetic information. RNA, bearing ribose and uracil and usually single-stranded, is more versatile and transient—acting as the working copies, catalysts, and regulators that translate the information in DNA into cellular function.
